description: basalt helps farmers decide what to plant next by testing crop rotations against 24 seasons of NASA weather at their location. See which rotations could keep soil covered longer, use less water or reduce weather risk. Season Strata shows when each rotation leaves soil bare or crops exposed to stress. Farmers can test warmer, wetter or drier conditions and see the evidence and uncertainty behind each comparison.
summary:
basalt is a decision-support tool that helps farmers and extension workers explore crop rotations for a specific location before making a change. It combines NASA POWER weather, MODIS vegetation and evapotranspiration data, GRACE-FO water storage and FIRMS fire records with global crop calendars and soil maps. A daily FAO-56 soil-water model then replays the current rotation and up to three alternatives through 24 real farming years, from 2001 to 2024.

Alternatives are generated by simple agronomic rules: filling bare periods with legumes or cover crops, replacing the most stressed crop, or alternating with a legume across years. Each one is checked against local season length, heat, frost and water. Every option is compared with the current rotation year by year on soil health practices, crop water use and weather risk, and comes with the reasons it was suggested, the evidence, its benefits, information gaps and the risks that need local review.

basalt is calibrated for Punjab, India, and uses global defaults elsewhere, with every validation check shown openly. It addresses the challenge directly: it makes NASA data usable for rotation decisions, shows how conditions have changed, and treats farmer judgment as the final word.
details:
What it does

Basalt compares crop rotations for a specific location. It reads the field's crop calendar from MODIS greenness data, then runs a daily soil-water model (FAO-56) driven by NASA POWER weather for every farming year from 2001 to 2024. Each alternative is compared with the current rotation in the same year, so results read as "better in 21 of 24 seasons" rather than an average.

What users see

1. Your field: 24 seasons stacked as layers, showing bare periods, heat at flowering, frost and heavy rain on bare soil, plus long-term trends and the regional groundwater trend from GRACE-FO.

2. Your options: one table comparing soil, water and weather risk for each option, with the five sections the challenge asks for: why suggested, evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks to check locally.

3. How sure are we: every validation check, including the ones that fail.

How alternatives are found

Four simple rules: fill the longest bare window with a legume or cover crop, swap the most stressed crop for another crop grown locally, alternate with a legume across years on single-season farms, or combine two of these. An option is only shown if it fits the local season, heat, frost and water.

Science and checks

The water model reproduces the FAO-56 worked example (3.88 vs 3.9 mm/day) and balances to within 0.1 mm every day. In Ludhiana the satellite-read calendar matched local dates within 13 days; in Malawi it was off by 38 days, and we show that as a failure. A sensitivity test varies the uncertain inputs, and anything that changes a result is listed under "check locally".

Scope and limits

It is calibrated for Punjab using Punjab Agricultural University guidance, and uses global defaults elsewhere (GGCMI crop calendars, SoilGrids soil). At Ludhiana, the global defaults agreed with the calibrated model on 12 of 12 verdicts. Soil health is scored from farming practices, not measured. Disease, nutrients and income are not modelled. Results are per location, not per field zone.

Why it matters

Most rotation tools rely on average weather and US-only data. Basalt runs wherever crops are grown and shows trade-offs honestly. In Punjab, adding summer moong helps the soil but needs more water and faces more heat. This gives farmers and extension officers a concrete basis for a conversation.

Tools

Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, pymannkendall, Playwright for screenshots. Code: https://github.com/vaibhavshakya11/basalt (MIT licence).
